interactions.summary: Jiang accepts the student's inside-outside reformulation and simplifies it into a direct model: intuition is a connection to the divine source that can be strengthened through love, faith, inquiry, debate, reading, and the pursuit of knowledge.

A participant reads Paradise 5 as Dante and Beatrice move into a brighter sphere, encounter splendors, and approach the figure who will answer from within excess light; Jiang then identifies the figure as Justinian and frames the coming canto as a history of Rome.

Jiang halts on the word 'gods' in heaven, says it should shock a Christian listener because paradise ought to be strictly monotheistic, and a student asks whether Dante is invoking the Greek gods he had already referenced earlier in the poem.

speaker_notes.note: The Paradise reading is noisy in places, but the scene movement is clear: Beatrice's speech ends, Dante enters a brighter sphere, and Justinian is introduced as the radiant speaker.
speaker_notes.suggested_speaker: Student reader followed by Jiang commentary

claims.claim: Jiang defines intuition as a person's connection to the divine or to the universe, saying it comes from the source rather than from isolated private subjectivity.
Jiang says the connection of intuition can be strengthened through a life of love, faith, reading, debate, inquiry, and the pursuit of knowledge.
Jiang explicitly rejects a science-versus-intuition split by saying that for Dante science and intuition are codependent and that real scientific insight requires intuition.
Jiang identifies the radiant figure in the new heavenly sphere as Justinian, the Byzantine emperor, and frames the next canto as Justinian's history of Rome.

Jiang argues that the appearance of the word 'gods' in heaven is deliberately jarring because a Christian listener expects strict monotheism, so the wording itself becomes evidence that Divine Comedy contains subversive pressure against a simple orthodox reading.
A student makes the implied reference explicit by asking whether the strange plural 'gods' points back to Dante's earlier invocations of Apollo and the Muses.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang stops hedging and says intuition is not just an inward feeling but a living connection to the divine source.
signature_moments.source_phrase: your intuition is ultimately your connection to the divine
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It converts the prior classroom back-and-forth into a direct metaphysical model rather than a mere study tip about scripture.

signature_moments.moment: Science and intuition become allies instead of enemies: Jiang says only through intuition can you truly be a scientist.
signature_moments.source_phrase: science and intuition are not mutually exclusive. they are codependent
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is a sharp Jiang-style reversal that joins rational inquiry to spiritual attunement instead of separating them.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang treats one four-letter word in heaven as a theological alarm bell: 'gods' should not be there.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's a word four letters guys four letter word that should not be in heaven
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns a tiny lexical detail into the hinge for reading Dante as quietly subversive from inside Christianity.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's term for the divine origin from which intuition comes and to which a person can become more strongly connected.
Jiang's description of the relationship between science and intuition in Dante: each depends on the other rather than canceling the other out.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet advances the seminar from an anti-literalist method claim into a stronger ontology of intuition as divine connection, then immediately applies that deeper reading style to a small textual shock in Paradise by treating 'gods' as evidence of Dante's subversive pressure inside Christian language.

uncertainty_notes.note: Part of the read-aloud Paradise passage is ASR-frayed, but the interpretive hinge does not depend on reconstructing every poetic line.
